title: Delhi Doctors Report GI Cancer Patients as Young as 15, Urge Air Pollution Research
excerpt: Sir Ganga Ram Hospital specialists told an international conference the pattern was uncommon five years ago — and stressed that a pollution link is a research question, not a proven cause.
body:
• Doctors at Delhi's Sir Ganga Ram Hospital told an international oncology conference they are now seeing gastrointestinal cancer patients as young as 15, a pattern they say was uncommon five years ago.
  • The experts stressed that air pollution has NOT been proven to cause these cancers; they are calling for India-specific research into PM2.5 and ground-level ozone.
  • A 2026 review of 70 studies linked long-term PM2.5 exposure to higher mortality from GI cancers, particularly colorectal cancer — an association, not proof of causation.
  • For families: persistent digestive symptoms in teenagers and young adults — unexplained weight loss, blood in stool, lasting abdominal pain — warrant a medical evaluation rather than watchful waiting.

Delhi's cancer specialists are asking a question they cannot yet answer: is the city's air doing damage below the lungs? At an international conference on gastrointestinal cancers this weekend, doctors from Sir Ganga Ram Hospital reported that their outpatient clinics are now seeing new GI cancer patients as young as 15 years old — cases they say were uncommon five years ago — and called for urgent research into air pollution as a possible factor.

"Cancer prevention can no longer be discussed only in terms of tobacco, diet and lifestyle," said Dr. Shyam Aggarwal, chairperson of medical oncology at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital and the conference's organising chairperson. "In our OPD we are now seeing new GI cancer patients as young as 15 years old which was uncommon 5 years ago. We must also pay attention to the environment in which people live."

What the evidence does — and does not — show

The doctors were explicit about the limits of the claim. The hospital's observation is a clinical pattern, not a population study: it does not by itself establish how widespread early-onset GI cancer is in Delhi, or what is causing the cases seen. Family history, genetic factors, diet, lifestyle and infections all remain established lines of inquiry for cancers of the stomach, colon and rectum.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2109656585945731468

The research discussed at the conference points to association rather than proof. A review published this year in Epidemiologic Reviews, covering 70 studies of air pollution and gastrointestinal disease, found that long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was associated with higher mortality from GI cancers, particularly colorectal cancer. A separate study in Nature Health, spanning 952 locations between 2000 and 2020, reported associations between PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide and ozone exposure and higher overall cancer risk. Neither establishes that pollution directly caused individual cancers.

"Cancer is a complex challenge that requires coordinated efforts across institutions, specialities and countries."

— Dr. D. S. Rana, Chairman, Sir Ganga Ram Hospital Trust Society

Why ozone is entering the conversation

Aggarwal also urged attention to ground-level ozone, a pollutant that receives far less public focus than particulate matter in Delhi's annual smog debate. The two-day conference, held on October 10 and 11 in New Delhi, was organised by Sir Ganga Ram Hospital with The Christie NHS Foundation Trust of the UK, and brought together Indian and international specialists on colorectal and other GI cancers. Punya Salila Srivastava, secretary of the Union Health and Family Welfare Ministry, attended as chief guest.

What this means for families

For diaspora readers with family in Delhi, the practical takeaway is narrower than the headline. There is no new screening guideline and no proven pollution-cancer verdict. What specialists are urging is earlier attention to symptoms: GI cancers in young patients are frequently diagnosed late because neither families nor doctors expect them. Persistent abdominal pain, blood in the stool, unexplained weight loss or a lasting change in bowel habits in a teenager or young adult should be evaluated, not waited out. The research demand is the story's real outcome — until India-specific studies on PM2.5, ozone and GI cancer are done, the link the doctors suspect will remain exactly that: suspected, and worth investigating. Reporting by NDTV and The Times of India.
